content: Henry Molaison, often referred to as H.M., was born in 1926 in Connecticut. He became one of the most studied patients in the history of neuroscience due to his profound memory impairment following brain surgery in 1953. His case has been pivotal in advancing our understanding of the relationship between brain structures and memory, as well as in the development of cognitive neuropsychology, a field that examines brain injuries to infer normal psychological functions. H.M. lived in a care facility in Hartford, Connecticut, where he continued to be the subject of scientific investigation. Audio recordings of his conversations with researchers from the 1990s were made public in 2007. H.M. suffered from severe epilepsy, which may have been caused by a bicycle accident at the age of seven, though this connection remains inconclusive. He experienced partial seizures for many years, which escalated to tonic-clonic seizures after he turned sixteen. By the age of 27, his seizures had become debilitating, leading him to seek treatment from Dr. William Scoville, a neurosurgeon at Hartford Hospital. Scoville identified H.M.'s medial temporal lobes (MTLs) as the source of his epilepsy and proposed surgical resection of these areas as a treatment. On September 1, 1953, Scoville performed the surgery, removing significant portions of H.M.'s medial temporal lobes on both sides of his brain. This included approximately two-thirds of his hippocampal formation, the parahippocampal gyrus (with complete destruction of the entorhinal cortex), and the amygdala. The remaining hippocampal tissue was atrophic and nonfunctional due to the loss of its primary sensory input from the entorhinal cortex. Additionally, parts of his anterolateral temporal cortex were removed. While the surgery successfully reduced the frequency and severity of H.M.'s seizures, it resulted in profound anterograde amnesia. Although his short-term memory remained intact, he was unable to form new long-term memories. He also experienced temporally graded retrograde amnesia, meaning he could not recall events from the three to four years preceding the surgery and had partial memory loss for events up to 11 years prior. However, his ability to form long-term procedural memories, such as learning new motor skills, remained intact. For example, he could learn tasks like mirror drawing but would have no recollection of having learned them. These findings were first reported in a landmark 1957 paper by Scoville and Brenda Milner. H.M.'s case has provided critical insights into the neural mechanisms underlying memory. His ability to perform tasks requiring short-term memory and procedural memory, but not long-term episodic memory, suggests that these memory systems are mediated by distinct brain regions. The fact that he could recall long-term memories from his distant past but not form new ones indicates that the processes of encoding and retrieval of long-term memories involve separate neural systems. His case has been instrumental in shaping theories about the role of the medial temporal lobes in memory formation, particularly in the encoding of semantic and episodic long-term memories. Despite his severe amnesia, H.M. retained normal intellectual abilities and language skills, indicating that these functions are independent of the medial temporal lobes. His working memory was also intact, as demonstrated by his ability to recall numbers over short intervals, performing as well as control subjects in such tasks. This supports the distinction between short-term and long-term memory systems and suggests that working memory does not rely on the medial temporal structures. H.M.'s preserved ability to acquire new motor skills was demonstrated in studies such as Milner's mirror-drawing task in the 1960s and Corkin's motor learning experiments in 1968. He also showed intact implicit memory, as evidenced by his performance in repetition priming tasks. These findings highlight the dissociation between declarative (explicit) and non-declarative (implicit) memory systems, with the latter relying on neural structures outside the medial temporal lobes. Remarkably, H.M. was able to construct a cognitive map of his residence, despite his severe anterograde amnesia. This ability is thought to be due to partially intact spatial processing networks, such as the posterior parahippocampal gyrus. He also demonstrated limited learning in tasks involving picture recognition and famous faces, particularly when provided with phonemic cues. These findings suggest that spared extrahippocampal regions may contribute to certain aspects of semantic and recognition memory. H.M.'s temporally graded retrograde amnesia provided valuable insights into the process of memory consolidation. He could recall childhood memories but struggled with events closer to the time of his surgery. This pattern suggests that older memories become independent of the medial temporal lobes over time, while more recent memories rely on these structures for consolidation. The medial temporal lobes are thought to facilitate the gradual transfer of memories to cortical regions, where they are stored more permanently. In summary, H.M.'s case has profoundly influenced our understanding of human memory, demonstrating the distinct roles of different brain regions in various memory processes. His contributions have led to the rejection of outdated theories and the development of new models of memory, particularly regarding the separation of declarative and non-declarative memory systems, the role of the medial temporal lobes in memory consolidation, and the neural basis of spatial memory.
